did_you_know.text: Did you know? Jehoshaphat returned safely to Jerusalem after the war, but his safe return did not cancel the prophetic criticism of his decisions.
Did you know? Jehu son of Hanani, known as the seer, went out to meet Jehoshaphat and rebuked him for helping the wicked and loving those who hate the Lord.
Did you know? Alongside his rebuke, Jehu also acknowledged Jehoshaphat’s good deeds: removing the Asherah poles and setting his heart on seeking God.
Did you know? Jehoshaphat went throughout the people’s towns, from Beersheba to the hill country of Ephraim, with the aim of bringing them back to the Lord, the God of their ancestors.
Did you know? After his spiritual reforms, Jehoshaphat appointed judges in all the fortified cities of Judah, city by city.

Did you know? Jehoshaphat reminded the judges that they were judging not only before human beings, but before the Lord; therefore, he required them to act in the fear of the Lord and with a sense of responsibility.
Did you know? The chapter explicitly forbids three major flaws in justice: wrongdoing, partiality, and accepting bribes.

Did you know? A central judicial system was established in Jerusalem, consisting of Levites, priests, and heads of families. It handled both matters concerning the Lord’s law and disputes among the people.

Did you know? The matters brought before the court included cases involving bloodshed, the law, commandments, statutes, and ordinances. Its role was also to warn the people so that they would not incur guilt before the Lord.

Did you know? Jehoshaphat divided the responsibilities among different leaders: Amariah the chief priest was responsible for matters concerning the Lord’s word, Zebadiah the ruler for matters concerning the king, and the Levites served as officers.
